subject: science
chapter_title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye

concepts.title: Cell: The Basic Unit of Life
concepts.definition: Every living body is built from microscopic blocks called cells, each bounded by a membrane and holding living matter; cells are too small for the naked eye, so a microscope reveals the invisible architecture of plants and animals.
concepts.key_idea: All living things are assemblies of cells - the smallest unit that shows life.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu102.txt lines 121-344 (what is a cell, microscope observation)
question_patterns: what is a cell and why is it called the basic unit of life
why is a microscope needed to see cells
name the outer boundary of a cell
how do cells of a plant leaf look under a microscope
who discovered cells and how
compare the sizes of cells with objects visible to the naked eye

solution_steps.explain: A cell is the smallest structure that carries out life processes.
Cell dimensions fall far below unaided eye resolution, about a tenth of a millimetre or less.
A microscope magnifies thin slices or peels to show cell walls, membranes and nuclei.

concepts.title: Levels of Organisation in Living Bodies
concepts.definition: Life is organised in layers: similar cells group into tissues, tissues cooperate as organs, organs team up into organ systems, and together they make the complete organism.
concepts.formula: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism
concepts.key_idea: Each level of organisation adds new functions built from the level below.
question_patterns: arrange cell, tissue, organ and organ system in the correct order
define a tissue with an example
give one example each of an organ and an organ system
why is an organ able to do more work than a single tissue
what level does a complete plant or animal represent
how do cells and tissues differ

solution_steps.explain: Cells of one kind doing one job form a tissue.
Tissues combine into organs, organs into organ systems.
All systems working together make one living organism.

concepts.title: Microorganisms: The Invisible Living World
concepts.definition: A whole world of living beings - bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses - stays hidden from the naked eye; these microorganisms live in soil, water, air and inside bodies, and only magnification reveals their shapes and movements.
concepts.key_idea: Microorganisms are everywhere, but only a microscope shows them.
question_patterns: name the major groups of microorganisms
where do microorganisms live
why are viruses considered on the border of living and non-living
which microorganism is used to make curd
how can we observe microorganisms in the classroom
why can microorganisms not be seen with the naked eye

solution_steps.explain: Bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses form the main microbial groups.
They inhabit soil, water, air, decaying matter and living bodies.
Microscope slides of pond water or curd reveal moving and fixed microbes.

concepts.title: Our Connection with Microbes: Use and Harm
concepts.definition: Microbes touch human life both ways - they ferment curd, bread and idli, decompose waste and fix soil nutrients, yet some cause diseases, food spoilage and infections, so hygiene and preservation manage their effects.
concepts.key_idea: The same invisible world can feed us or make us ill - handling decides which.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu102.txt lines 522-807 (how are we connected to microbes)
question_patterns: give three useful roles of microorganisms in daily life
how do microbes spoil food and how can spoilage be prevented
name two diseases caused by microorganisms
how do microbes help in cleaning the environment
why is curd formation an example of useful microbes
what habits reduce the harm from harmful microbes

solution_steps.explain: Separate helpful uses such as fermentation and decomposition from harmful disease and spoilage.
Boiling, salting, refrigeration and hygiene control unwanted microbes.
Human life depends on managed coexistence with the microbial world.
